lines: Haskett: You. Wayfarer. You've got the look of someone who needs money and has no opinions.
Haskett: My miners are on strike down in Shatterfloor. Sitting on my ore. Singing. Badly.
Haskett: Go down, have a word, have a fight. I pay well. In a manner of speaking.
Haskett: Mine's past the square, down the hole. Mind the floor. It's cheaper than the miners.
Haskett: Strike's broken? Lovely. Ore's moving, my heart's singing. In tune, unlike them.
Haskett: Now. About your pay.
Haskett: Sided with the diggers, did you? I could tell. You've got dirt on your conscience.
Haskett: Prawle! Show our guest the way out. The long way.
Haskett's office is empty. A note on the desk: 'Mine sold. To myself. Under my other name. - H.'
Haskett: Pleasure doing business. Mostly my pleasure.
You read his pay ledger in the mine. You ask for coin, not company scrip.
Haskett: Clever. I hate clever. Here, real coin. It hurts me more than it hurts you.
Haskett pays you in company scrip. Good only in his own shop. Which closed yesterday.
Haskett: And here's the bill for the lamp oil you burned down there. Business, you understand.
Paid in scrip
Foreman Haskett hired you to break the Shatterfloor strike.
He paid the miners in scrip for years. He tried the same on you.
Dory: Haskett sent you. I can smell his cologne on your boots. It's called Greed, number five.
Dory: He wants to flood this gallery for the insurance. Nests and all. We sit here, he can't.
Dory: So. Whose side are you on, Wayfarer?
Dory shows you Haskett's pay ledger. Every wage is paid in 'scrip'. Every page has a doodle of a boat.
Dory: The boat's for when he runs. He draws it every day. Planning ahead, our Haskett.
Dory: Then go and tell him. Watch his face go the colour of old cheese.
Dory: Come back when he's run. And he will run. Men who draw boats always do.
Dory: Still here? Haskett won't run from you standing in my mine.
Dory: He ran! Boat and all! You should have seen the miners. Grown women weeping into their pickaxes.
Dory: We passed the hat for you. It's a good hat.

choices.text: Keep it for the miners' families.

lines: Dory: One more thing, love.
Dory: The Marrovels offered to buy the mine this morning. I was going to say yes.
Dory: Then you gave the hat back. Now I can't, can I? Curse you and your manners. Take this instead.
Dory gives you a Revival Leaf, wrapped in a page of Haskett's ledger.
Dory: I sold the mine to the Marrovels this morning. Good price. Better than Haskett's boat.
Dory: Strike's over. We're all employees now. Cheers for the help, love. Truly.
Dory: Strike's on. Unless you're from Haskett. You've got a bit of a Haskett face.
Someone has chalked SCAB on the wall, with an arrow pointing at where you stand.
Dory: Morning, colleague. Clock in, clock out, keep your head down. Marrovel rules.
The miners' hat
You helped Dory Flint's strike run Haskett out of Copperfold.
Then Dory looked at the Marrovels' offer, and at you, and chose.
Dory: Fine. Go tell Haskett. Tell him we'll be back on the same day his pay is.
Dory: Never, in other words.
Dory: Off you pop. Union rules: losers make the tea.
Prawle: I'm not paid enough for this. I'm not paid at all. Scrip, mate. Scrip.
Behind him, Haskett is already climbing into a cart marked 'Definitely Not Haskett'.
Prawle: Exit's that way. Mind the step. There's no step. Just me.
Dunk: Twenty years down here. Haskett gave me a clock for it. The clock is also scrip.
Dunk: Scab! Haskett's scab! I can tell by the walk. Shifty knees.
Dunk: Knees were right, though.
Gwen: My Shalebat hasn't seen daylight in a year. It thinks the sun is a rumour.
Gwen: No one crosses the line. Not even a cute one with a rucksack.
Gwen: The line's moved. Apparently.
Wendle: Dory keeps the strike fund. I've never seen it. Nobody has. It's a very secret fund.
Wendle: I sing the strike songs. All forty verses. Fight me or hear them.
Wendle: Verse forty-one: the one where we lost.
Odette: Two husbands, dear. Both terribly unlucky. One fell into a well. The other fell into a different well.
Odette: Now I'm engaged to Lemuel in Wrenhollow. Sweet man. Owns a house. Big one.
Odette: Take him this tonic, would you? For his nerves. Don't read the label, it's personal.
The label, in Odette's neat hand: 'For Lemuel. Sleep tight. Sign here.' There is a dotted line. You pocket the label.
Odette: Reading other people's labels. Your mother would be ashamed. I would know, I'm very ashamed of most people.
Odette: Wrenhollow is past Quillbrook. Lemuel's the one with the hopeful face. Hurry, the tonic goes off.
Odette: He's asleep? Already? Bless him. And the deed's in my name by morning. Love is so efficient.
Odette: Here, for your trouble. And dear: your name is on the delivery slip. Just so you know.
Odette: Lemuel watered a fern with my tonic. The fern is asleep. Do you know what ferns cost?
Odette: I'll have to do this the old-fashioned way. Through you.
Odette: Shoo. I'm planning a wedding. Or a funeral. Same caterers.
Odette: Lemuel forgave me. Wedding's Sunday. You're not invited, but your Spirlings can carry the train.
Odette: Fine! I'll marry him properly. Awake. Ugh.
Odette: Sleep tight, dear. No label needed.
The Watch comes asking about a sleeping man and a missing deed. You show them the label in Odette's hand.
They fine her, not you. She waves at you from across the pier with two fingers. Not a friendly number.
The Watch comes asking about a sleeping man and a missing deed. The delivery slip has your name on it.
You pay the courier's fine. Odette buys a new hat. It's a lovely hat.
The widow's tonic
You carried Widow Pinch's tonic to her fiance Lemuel. He slept for four days.
His house changed hands while he snored. Your name was on the slip.
Lemuel: A present from Odette? She's so thoughtful. Last week she measured me. For a suit, she said.
Lemuel: A long box of a suit, but she's very modern.
Lemuel drinks it in one go. 'Tastes like almonds and paperwork,' he says, and falls asleep mid-smile.
Lemuel: Don't drink it? Nonsense. Odette knits me socks. Murderers don't knit. Well. Not socks.
He pours a drop on his fern to prove you wrong. The fern yawns and goes to sleep.
Lemuel: ...Take this. And maybe stand between us for a while.
Lemuel: YOU. The tonic courier. I slept four days. She sold my house. And my hat. And my fern.
Lemuel: I can't fight Odette. I'm terrified of Odette. But you I can manage.
Lemuel: Odette says I worry too much. She says it while sharpening things.
Lemuel: I sleep in the library now. The books don't drug me.
Lemuel: Odette and I are getting married on Sunday! She forgave me. She forgave you too, she said. In a voice.
Lemuel: Fair. I'd have done the same for a strong tonic.
Lemuel: Now we're even. Mostly. I'm still homeless.
Jinks: There you are. I've been sitting on these steps so long the lamps know my name.
Jinks: Bad news: I'm broke. Worse news: the man who paid me to slow you down wants his money back.
Jinks: One more round. For old times. And for my pride, which is also broke.
Jinks: Fine. You want to know who paid me? Brennick. The lender in Brindlewick.
Jinks: He sells names. Yours fetched a good price in Corvane. Mine's next, now I've talked.
Jinks: Find me in Copperfold. I need to leave town, and leaving costs money.
Jinks: Ha! At least I'm still better than someone. Very cheering.
Jinks: Brennick's collectors are two towns behind me and gaining. I need two hundred coins for a cart.
Jinks: I'll pay you back double. Swear on my mum. Well. On someone's mum.
Jinks drinks it in one go and tells you his real name. It is much worse than Jinks.
Jinks: Nobody's ever bought me a drink without wanting something. Do you want something? You do, don't you.
Jinks takes the coins, grins, and is gone. A minute later a large woman with a ledger blocks the road.
Dunmore: Jinks sold me your whereabouts for a head start. Says you owe Brennick. Everyone owes Brennick.
A week later a parcel comes for you: four hundred coins and a note. 'Double, like I said. Don't tell anyone I'm honest. - J.'
Jinks pays you back the same evening, exact to the coin. He looks surprised at himself.
Dunmore: Fine. I'll write you down as 'paid in bruises'. Brennick accepts those. Barely.
Dunmore: Interest is due on Tuesday. Every Tuesday. Forever.
A cart for Jinks
You lent Jinks Calloway two hundred coins to run from Brennick's collectors.
He bought his head start with your name instead.
Sprocket: Copperfold bounties! Approved by the Bailiff, which is me. Very official. Mostly stamps.
The board is empty. A fresh notice is pinned in the corner, half written. It has your name on it.
The cheap end of the board. Somebody has corrected the spelling in red.

choices.text: Wanted: Old Gristmouth, a Talusk that eats cart wheels
Wanted: Penny Dreadful, who returns purses empty

lines: The dear end of the board. The ink is still wet on one of them.

choices.text: Wanted: The Kettle Brothers, who sell the same goat twice
Wanted: Ex-Bailiff Holloway, for knowing too much

lines: Old Gristmouth spits out a wheel nut and lumbers off into the scree.
Old Gristmouth eats one of your bootlaces. With relish.
Penny: Here's your purse back. Empty, as is tradition.
Penny: Lovely purse. I'll return it. Eventually. Empty.
Kettle: The goat was ours both times! It just kept coming home!
Kettle: Want to buy a goat? Very loyal. Comes back to us.
Holloway: Sprocket takes bribes from Haskett. I reported it. Now I'm on his board.
Holloway: Next week it'll be your name. Sprocket never runs out of villains. He makes them.
Holloway: Run, kid. Before he pins you up too.
A wanted poster with your face on it. The artist was unkind about your nose. REWARD: 40 coins. Insulting.
WANTED: the lighthouse brat. Crimes: trespassing, Rift-meddling, looking smug. You tear it down.
A poster: 'Seen this Wayfarer? Do not approach. Do not feed.' Someone has drawn a moustache on you. It suits you.
WANTED, ALIVE. 'Alive' is underlined three times, then crossed out once. You take it down quickly.
A soggy poster in the reeds. Your face, and below it: 'Last seen being helpful. Suspicious.'
A poster nailed to a post. In small print: 'Printed by Gorrie and Sons, Brindlewick. Bulk discounts.'
WANTED for questioning. The questions are listed. Question one: 'Why?' Question two: 'Why though?'
A fresh poster. The paste is still wet. Somebody put this up an hour ago, and they knew you'd come this way.
Gorrie: Psst. Your face is on posters all over Veydal. Not my work, I swear. Well. Not my idea.
Gorrie: Tear down all eight before some bounty hunter reads one. Bring them here. I pay for paper.
Gorrie: All eight, mind. A single poster is a rumour. Eight is a reputation.
Gorrie: All eight! Lovely. Here's your pay.
Gorrie: Between us: Clerk Brannagh ordered them. I printed them. Then I paid you to take them down.
Gorrie: Paid twice for the same paper. Printing is a beautiful trade. He's ordered a second run, by the way.
Gorrie: Second run's at the press. Different nose this time. Kinder, I think.
Crane: Someone burned the town debt book. Every debt Wrenhollow owes the Marrovels, gone in one night.
Crane: The Marrovels want a name by the end of the week, or they'll pick one themselves. They are not careful pickers.
Crane: Ask Tibbs, my apprentice. Ask Fay, the lamplighter in Quillbrook. Look at my shelves. Then tell me who.
Crane: Well? You've asked around. You've rummaged through my shelves. Who burned it?
Crane: I knew it! I'll send the name to the Marrovels tonight. Case closed. Here's your fee.
Crane: Don't look so glum. Somebody had to be guilty. Better them than someone important. Like me.
Crane: Me? Burn my own book? How dare you. How did you know? No. Don't answer.
Crane: Nobody leaves this library with that idea in their head.
Crane: Page one. My name. Nine hundred coins to the Marrovels. I only meant to burn page one.
Crane: The rest caught. Books are terribly flammable. Nobody warns you.
Crane: Take the reward from the shelf. Tibbs will run the library now. Heaven help the books.
Crane: Shh. This is a library. Losers are very quiet here.
Crane: Tibbs in town, Fay in Quillbrook, and my shelves. Clues are like debts, dear. They turn up.
Crane: The Marrovels were very pleased with the name. They took it away in a sack.
Tibbs: The Archivist is copying debt books by hand now. Forever. It's her sentence. She's quite good at it.
Tibbs: The fire? I was asleep. In the library. On the debt book. It's very comfy, it's the thickest book.
Tibbs: The Archivist woke me and sent me home early. She had a lamp and a very big can of oil. For reading, she said.
Tibbs: I dust books. Books don't dust back. It's a lonely trade.
Tibbs: They took Fay away. Poor Fay. I mean. Better her than me. Is that bad?
Tibbs: Sacked. For a fire I slept through. The Marrovels want me to work it off. In a mine.
Tibbs: I'm Archivist now! The pay is terrible and the last one is still in the building.
Fay: Me? I light lamps. I don't burn books. Different trade. Similar smell.
Fay: Mind you, the library bought a whole can of lamp oil from me that day. On account. Crane signed for it.
Fay: Every lamp on this brook, lit by me. Every lamp that goes out, blamed on me.
Fay: The Marrovels say I owe them a library. I've started saving. Twelve coins so far.
A scorched page under the shelf. One line survived: 'Owed to the Marrovels: Archivist M. Crane, 900 coins.'
